questions.:question/problem:
Express $$
\displaystyle {\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)-{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)
$$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{\cos }^{2}⁡x-{\sin }^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)-{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:
Express

$$
\cos^2 23^\circ-\sin^2 23^\circ
$$

as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).
$$

Substitute $x=23^\circ$ and double the angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^2 23^\circ-\sin^2 23^\circ
&=\cos(2\cdot23^\circ) \\
&=\cos 46^\circ.
\end{aligned}
$$

The angle doubles; there is no extra coefficient outside the cosine.

questions.:question/problem:
Express

$$
2\cos^4 19^\circ-2\sin^4 19^\circ
$$

as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Factor out $2$, then use the difference of squares $a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$ with $a=\cos^2 19^\circ$ and $b=\sin^2 19^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&2\cos^4 19^\circ-2\sin^4 19^\circ \\
&\quad=2\left(\cos^4 19^\circ-\sin^4 19^\circ\right) \\
&\quad=2\left(\cos^2 19^\circ-\sin^2 19^\circ\right)
\left(\cos^2 19^\circ+\sin^2 19^\circ\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The Pythagorean identity gives $\cos^2 19^\circ+\sin^2 19^\circ=1$. Therefore,

$$
2\cos^4 19^\circ-2\sin^4 19^\circ
=2\left(\cos^2 19^\circ-\sin^2 19^\circ\right).
$$

Now apply $\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)$ with $x=19^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\left(\cos^2 19^\circ-\sin^2 19^\circ\right)
&=2\cos(2\cdot19^\circ) \\
&=2\cos 38^\circ.
\end{aligned}
$$

The fourth powers form a difference of squares, not the square of a difference. Factor before using the double-angle formula.

2\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)-2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)
$$

as a single trigonometric ratio.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First factor out the common coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&2\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)-2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right) \\
&\quad=2\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall $\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)$. With $x=\frac{\pi}{14}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)\right)
&=2\cos\left(2\cdot\frac{\pi}{14}\right) \\
&=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Keep the common factor $2$ outside the cosine; only the angle inside doubles.

$$
4\left(\cos^{2}\left(12^\circ\right)-\sin^{2}\left(12^\circ\right)\right).

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).

$$
\begin{aligned}
&4\left(\cos^{2}\left(12^\circ\right)-\sin^{2}\left(12^\circ\right)\right) \\

Only the angle doubles; the common coefficient stays outside the cosine.

Recall the **double-angle formula for cosine**:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{31}$ and double the angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&12\left(\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{31}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{31}\right)\right) \\
&=12\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi}{31}\right) \\
&=12\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{31}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Only the angle doubles; the common coefficient stays outside the cosine.
